title: Directional word-transmission pilot
scope: Exploratory calibration only; not a proof of common ancestry or borrowing.

method.phonetic_score: Weighted edit similarity over broad sound classes. Vowel-to-vowel substitutions are discounted; s~sh/ʃ, k~g~x~h, t~d and other close classes are cheaper than unrelated substitutions. Insertions/deletions are penalized.
method.semantic_score: Meanings are compared on a small transparent concept graph: cause -> efficacy -> authority -> divine agency, with number-eight and enclosure kept separate. This is a pilot ontology, not a full semantic model.
method.calibration: Known historical developments are treated as positive controls. Candidate links are scored only after those controls are fixed.
method.warning: Short words can resemble each other by chance. Candidate percentile values here are only against this curated pilot control set, not against all world languages.

sources.label: Yoruba àṣẹ meaning and derivation
sources.note: à- + ṣẹ 'come to pass / take effect'; IPA approximately /à.ʃɛ̄/.

sources.label: Yoruba cultural description of ase
sources.note: Describes ase as power, authority, command and the power to make things come to pass.

sources.label: Eight etymology
sources.note: Old English eahta < Proto-Germanic *akhto < PIE *okto(u); cognates include Greek okto and Latin octo.

sources.label: Æsir background
sources.note: Old Norse áss / plural Æsir from Proto-Germanic *ansuz.

positive_controls.note: Eight -> eighth branch; demonstrates kt -> gd-type reshaping.
Proto-Germanic divine-being term -> Old Norse áss.

candidates.note: Phonetically scores inside the range of several true controls. Semantically both occupy efficacy/authority/divine-agency territory. However Yoruba àṣẹ has a transparent internal derivation from ṣẹ 'come to pass/take effect', and no transmission chain to Germanic is currently known.

candidates.verdict: plausible resemblance, not evidence of descent
candidates.note: The phonetic score is comparable to the *ansuz -> áss positive control, but the semantic relationship is looser and the historical bridge is missing.
A one-way transition is mechanically plausible under the broad scoring model, but this does not establish chronology or borrowing.

conclusion: The known eight/octo/ogdo lineage validates that substantial surface change can preserve identity, including the striking okt -> ogd development. The àṣẹ -> áss candidate scores within the broad phonetic range of genuine historical controls and has a coherent semantic path through efficacy/authority/divine agency. However, the Yoruba word is internally analyzable as à- + ṣẹ 'come to pass/take effect', and no historical contact chain currently connects it to Proto-Germanic *ansuz. Therefore the experiment upgrades the pair from 'mere visual resemblance' to 'worth targeted historical testing', but does not support claiming common ancestry or borrowing yet.
